common_name: Arbosana Olive (Compact Cold-Hardy High-Density Oil Olive)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Arbosana is largely self-fertile though yields improve with a compatible pollinizer such as Arbequina nearby, and it tolerates somewhat colder winters than many other olive cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; avoid over-fertilizing or over-watering, since moderate stress improves oil quality. Arbosana is another small Spanish olive variety, alongside Arbequina, widely adopted in modern super-high-density olive orchards for its compact habit, precocious and heavy bearing, and good cold hardiness relative to larger traditional olive cultivars. The small fruit yields a well-regarded, balanced, mildly fruity oil, and the tree's naturally smaller size makes it practical for large containers and compact home landscapes, similar in scale to Arbequina but noted for handling occasional colder winter dips slightly better. Harvest olives as they shift from green to purple-black for oil production in late fall to early winter, or pick green and cure in brine for table olives. Established trees are drought-tolerant and need minimal fertilization.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Olive Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Olive Production in Texas

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Manzanillo is largely self-fertile though a compatible pollinizer such as Mission improves fruit set, and it grows into a larger, traditional-sized tree than compact modern cultivars like Arbequina.

directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant and should not be over-fertilized or over-watered. Manzanillo is a classic Spanish olive cultivar and the most widely grown table olive variety in the world, valued for its large, plump, meaty fruit with a favorable flesh-to-pit ratio that makes it the standard choice for brine-cured green and black table olives found in grocery stores worldwide. The tree bears heavily and reliably, and while it can also be pressed for oil, its primary use and reputation is as a table olive. Harvest green in fall for green-cured olives, or let fruit ripen to black for black-cured olives, then cure in brine or lye solution for several weeks to months to remove natural bitterness before eating; olives are inedible straight off the tree. The tree grows to a more traditional, larger size than modern compact cultivars, so allow ample space.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Olive Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Olive Production in Texas

common_name: Picholine Olive (French Dual-Purpose Table and Oil Olive)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Picholine benefits from a compatible pollinizer nearby for the best fruit set, and it is somewhat more cold-tolerant than many olive cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant and should not be over-fertilized or over-watered. Picholine is a classic French olive cultivar from the Languedoc region, valued as a dual-purpose variety producing both high-quality table olives — elongated, firm, green-cured olives with a distinctive nutty flavor — and good oil with a peppery, herbaceous character typical of southern French olive oils. The tree is notably vigorous and relatively cold-hardy for an olive, tolerating brief winter dips better than some more tender cultivars, which has made it a popular choice for marginal olive-growing climates. Harvest green in fall for classic Picholine table olives, curing in a lye or brine solution over several weeks to remove bitterness, or allow fruit to ripen further for oil pressing in early winter.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Olive Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Olive Production in Texas
